attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post. He asserts this himself and is not quoting anyone.

semantics.note: Naming LLMs as the systems fits the CNET/ChatGPT context. The proposition keeps 'inherently', 'starting to' and 'too many'. 'Too many' is evaluative and cannot be scored.

contract.note: Fair, ordinary reading: people are starting to rely on systems whose design does not reliably separate true from false. The contract correctly says observed errors alone do not prove an inherent limitation, and that use is not the same as reliance.

evidence.note: January 2023 preprint reports that ChatGPT invents facts, such as nonexistent laws. This partly supports the reliability concern but does not show the limitation is design-linked or inherent.
The same paper says ChatGPT sometimes declines questions outside its knowledge. This qualifies an absolute reading but does not show reliable truth discrimination.

January 2023 survey: almost 30% of professionals had used AI at work, described as early experimenting. This shows use, not reliance on factual accuracy, so it does not meet the 'count on' requirement.

reviews.rationale: The support condition needs a design-linked inability to track truth plus evidence that people relied on these systems for factual work. The packet shows fabrication but not that it is inherent, and it shows workplace experimentation rather than reliance. Nothing contradicts the claim either. The packet does not settle it, so the outcome is unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus says it himself ('Fact is...'). He adopts Mackworth's finding as his own claim rather than just reporting it.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the general claim about human limits and the credit to Mackworth, with no restriction added. The surrounding text ('can't pay attention forever') confirms it is about sustained vigilance.

contract.note: Reading the claim as unreliable continuous vigilance during long monitoring is ordinary and matches the context. It does not stretch the claim for or against the speaker.

evidence.note: A 2011 peer-reviewed experiment found vigilance performance fell steeply over time. Brief task switches prevented the decline, but that is a workaround, not proof of flawless continuous attention.

reviews.rationale: The support condition is published evidence of declining vigilance during long monitoring. e1 shows exactly that. The finding that mental breaks prevent the decline does not show reliably flawless, uninterrupted monitoring, so it does not meet the contradiction condition. The claim holds on the contract's fair, ordinary reading.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The main 'should know' clause is normative and was rightly left out. The 'about to head into' clause is an unhedged forecast with no date.

contract.note: The contract adds no deadline or threshold, and it says failure to occur by a date chosen by the evaluator cannot contradict the claim. Reading 'ubiquitous' as commonplace everyday and professional use is fair.

evidence.note: Stanford HAI summary: 78% of surveyed organisations used AI in 2024. This covers organisations only, not everyday use across society, so it is not a conclusive broad assessment.
Pew, early 2025: 34% of US adults had ever used ChatGPT and 66% had not. This covers one product in one country and only ever-use.
Google's own blog post admits inaccurate AI Overviews. It is a company disclosure showing errors in one feature only.

reviews.rationale: The forecast has no deadline. Under the contract it can be settled early only by a broad, dated assessment showing commonplace use across everyday and professional settings together with continuing errors. The packet has only partial evidence: organisational adoption, use of one product in the US, and one company's error admission. None meets the early-resolution rule, so the forecast stays unresolved.
